subtitle: Lesson 1 · Cloud Security Posture at Scale

eyebrow: The line moves with the service model

steps.label: IaaS — Azure VMs, EC2
steps.sub: customer owns guest OS, patching, NSGs/security groups, everything above the hypervisor

steps.label: PaaS — Azure SQL DB, App Service, RDS, Lambda
steps.sub: provider manages OS/engine/runtime; customer owns data, access, service config

steps.label: SaaS — Microsoft 365
steps.sub: provider owns almost everything; customer owns identity, data, tenant config

code:
# Azure VM / AWS EC2 (IaaS)
# Provider: datacenter, host hardware, hypervisor
# Customer: guest OS patches, NSGs/security groups,
#           identity to the instance, anything you install

# Azure SQL Database / AWS RDS (PaaS)
# Provider: OS patching, database engine, availability
# Customer: firewall rules, data, access configuration
caption: Same provider, same cloud — a different "your job" list for each service.

code:
# Exposed S3 bucket -> customer-side misconfiguration
# Azure SQL DB with open firewall -> customer-side misconfiguration
# Equifax (2017) -> unpatched customer-managed software
#
# In each case: provider infrastructure was never breached.
# The customer's half of the line was.
caption: This is exactly why CIS Benchmarks test customer-side controls, not provider infrastructure.

eyebrow: Before you deploy any new service

steps.label: Identify the service model
steps.sub: IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS — a starting point, not the final answer

steps.label: Read that service's own security baseline
steps.sub: Microsoft Learn security baseline page, or AWS's shared responsibility docs for that service

steps.label: Don't generalize across services
steps.sub: Lambda's boundary differs from EC2's even though both are AWS compute

subtitle: What actually changes when you're responsible for Azure and AWS at once.
